Learning from a frozen robot log: three ways it breaks

A fixed robot dataset can mislead a learner in two different ways: a hole, where it asks about actions nobody tried, and mistakes, where it copies bad demonstrations. Stay close to the data for the first, and weight actions by the reward for the second.

Say you have a log of a robot arm picking up a mug. Several operators drove it, some good and some clumsy, and the log is frozen: you can't run the robot again. You want a policy that grasps better than the average person in there. Normally a learner scores each recorded move by its reward plus its own guess of what happens next. If a guess is wrong, it tries the move and finds out. Here it can't, and that breaks learning in three unrelated ways. From the outside they all look the same: the robot grasps badly.

Let's start with the missing action. The critic (Q, a network that predicts how much reward follows an action) scores a slow descent 4 and a fast descent 3, and the log holds those moves 60 and 40 times. Then it scores a sideways sweep 9. Nobody ever tried the sweep! Taking the max over actions picks exactly that guess, which Fujimoto, Meger and Precup call extrapolation error. The second failure is a log that is accurate and full of operator mistakes, so anything that copies the log copies those too. The third is a log that lies. The board walks one mug state through all three, with made-up numbers you can check by hand.

Do real measurements agree? Mostly. In robomimic's square-nut task (Mandlekar et al., 2021; best training success rate, averaged over three seeds), adding 100 demonstrations from worse operators to 100 from better ones dropped plain BC from 58.7% to 46.7% success. More data gave a worse policy, which is what we'd expect if copying also copies mistakes. Give the cloning policy a memory of earlier observations (BC-RNN) and the result reverses, from 66.0% to 73.3%, and that comparison doesn't tell us why. In the Breaking Bellman two-link reaching simulation (three seeds, final tip distance to the target), a log of 50 good-controller and 50 random-command episodes put IQL at 0.22 m and AWR at 0.57 m. Both weight actions by advantage, yet their complete training procedures ended far apart. Swap in 100 clean controller episodes and plain copying wins: deterministic BC finishes 0.065 m from the target against 0.12 m for IQL. DDPG, which picks actions by climbing its own critic, finishes 0.84 m away.

If I had that mug log, I'd audit the records before training anything, because every method on the board takes the transitions at their word. Then I'd train plain BC as the baseline, since it is hard to beat on clean demonstrations, and check where the critic's favorite actions sit relative to the data. Only after that is it worth arguing about β.
